newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan elections go down to wire.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan elections go down to wire.

text.p: Right-wing populist Arnoldo Aleman held a narrow lead over surging left-wing rival Daniel Ortega in a poll released on Monday ahead of Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential election.
The CID-Gallup poll, the last before the election, gave Aleman of the Liberal Alliance 40.5 percent and Ortega of the left-wing Sandinista Front 37.9 percent, followed by 21 lesser candidates.

"It's not a tie. We predict Aleman as the winner, but we think that Ortega has an outside chance at winning," Carlos Denton, the president of CID-Gallup Costa Rica, told Reuters. "With nine percent of those polled saying they will decide who to vote for when they arrive at the voting booth and a 2.7 margin of error, the election could easily slide to Ortega."

Aleman, whose victory seemed assure only months ago, has seen his lead over Ortega in CID-Gallup polls dwindle from 17 percent at the start of 1996 to 2.6 percent today, while Ortega's popularity has soared from 21 percent to 38 percent, partly due to a smooth campaign that has changed his image from the fiery Marxist revolutionary who governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990 to a moderate social democrat who accepts the free market.

Denton also attributed Ortega's growing popularity to discontent with Nicaragua's economic problems. "If your perception is that your family is better off than in 1995, you're more likely to be an Aleman supporter. If your family is worse off, you're more likely to be an Ortega supporter," Denton said.
Since the majority of Nicaraguans are poor, this has led to a surge in support for Ortega, he said.
The poll also minimized the threat of election fraud, with 61 percent of those polled saying there was little or no possibility of fraud.

In contrast to Ortega's moderate dialogue, Aleman has maintained a frontal attack on his rival, reminding voters of the Sandinista government in the 1980s when Ortega censored the press, confiscated private property and fought an eight-year civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels.
Aleman, the portly former mayor of Managua, has been hurt by the perception his virulent anti-Sandinista stance would undermine efforts at national reconciliation.
CID-Gallup polled 1,318 people across Nicaragua on Oct. 1-8 and has a margin of error of 2.7 percentage points.
